:topic/_next.:topic/title: The Sum Rule for Indefinite Integrals

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=3x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3x+1)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {u}^{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{u}^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(3x+1)^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{12}(3x+1)^{4}+C] & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(3x+1)^{4}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 4(3x+1)^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x+1)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3x+1)^{3}\cdot 3 \\  & =(3x+1)^{3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Positive Integer Exponent

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\displaystyle\int 2(1-x)^{-3} \,  \textrm{d}x .
$$

Let $u=1-x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =  -\textrm d u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2(1-x)^{-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{u}^{-3}\cdot (-1)\text{d}u \\  & =-2\int {u}^{-3}\text{d}u \\  & =-2\cdot \frac{{u}^{-2}}{-2}+C \\  & ={u}^{-2}+C \\  & =(1-x)^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(1-x)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-2(1-x)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-x)+0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{(1-x)^{3}}\cdot (-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{(1-x)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\displaystyle\int(1-5x)^{1/2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Now, we let $u=1-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = -\dfrac 1 5 \textrm d u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (1-5x)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{1/2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{15}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{15}(1-5x)^{3/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(1-5x)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(1-5x)^{3}}+C] & =-\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\sqrt{(1-5x)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(1-5x)^{3/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(1-5x)^{1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-5x)+0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}(1-5x)^{1/2}\cdot (-5) \\  & =(1-5x)^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
